newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian pensions under strain as population ages.
newsitem.headline: Italian pensions under strain as population ages.

text.p: Italy's state pension system is coming under growing strain as the economy languishes and unemployment rises, forcing a shrinking working population to maintain a growing army of elderly people.
And nearly two years after reforms to the deficit-ridden system were hailed as a turning point, employers are warning Prime Minister Romano Prodi of a crisis ahead.

"We are unhappy with the reforms because the country was led to believe that the pensions problem had been solved," said Carlo Callieri, the President of the Italian employers' federation Confindustria.

Prodi has said he will a honour a pledge made in a pension reform deal in 1995 not to touch present arrangements until next year. Trade unions have threatened mass protests if changes to the system are brought forward.
At the heart of the problem is Italy's extremely low birth rate, which threatens over time to shrink the working population while average life expectancy has never been higher.

Italy already has one of the highest "dependency ratios" -- a measure of the elderly in proportion to the working population -- in the western world and demographers expect it to rise in the years ahead.
"We have 18 million pensions which are being paid for by 21 million working people," said Callieri.
Critics argue that the state pension system, even after the 1995 reforms, is simply beyond Italy's means as it pays out pensions worth up to 80 percent of final salary.
On present trends, Italy's pensions bill is set to climb by 50 percent in 2010 before doubling again by 2030, according to figures compiled by Milan business daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
Meanwhile, Italy's population between the ages of 15 and 70 is seen falling gently from 42.86 million in 1995 to 41.26 million in 2010 before plunging to 36.68 million in 2030, Il Sole 24 Ore said.

Like many European countries, Italy operates a so-called "pay-as-you-go" pension system under which handouts to the retired are paid from contributions drawn from those in work and from their employers.
The system flourished in the 1960s when the economy boomed and Italy enjoyed something approaching full employment for the first time in its recent history.
With a high birth rate and a growing labour force the state pensions institute, INPS, was able to guarantee pensions for practically everybody and to balance its books.

Today INPS is running an annual deficit of around 80 trillion lire ($50.31 billion), which has to be plugged with massive injections of cash from the Treasury. The deficit is bloated by the institute's obligation to grant basic pensions to poor people who have paid no contributions into the system.

Many believe the Dini reforms, which came into force at the beginning of 1996, are too slow to take effect, place too heavy a burden on those in work and on their employers and will not cut deep enough into a widening deficit in the years ahead.
"The Dini law is not enough," said Giulio Tremonti, a former Budget minister in the centre-right administration led by media magnate-turned-politician Silvio Berlusconi in 1994.
"This system takes away from those who work without guaranteeing a future for those who do not work," he said.
The main innovation of the Dini reform was to change the way the value of benefits are calculated when people retire and start to draw a pension.

The new system, which will not become fully effective until 2030, will base old age pensions on the value of contributions paid into the system over an individual's entire working life. Until now pension payouts reflect salary levels in the final years of employment.

This means that a generation of young Italians is growing up who cannot rely on the pension arrangements granted to their parents. The government recently passed legislation allowing companies to set up funds for pensions.
"For young people it is going to be a necessity," said Sergio Corbello, President of Assoprevidenza, the pension funds association.
